summary: Proposes changing the link function of the TENEX operating system to give a better user interface. The author says BBN had no complaints about the current version, asks for quick feedback, and promises to share the new version once tried.

plainLanguage.summary: A programmer wants to change how one feature of an operating system works, asks if anyone minds, and says it should take only a couple of hours.

subtitle: Proposal to improve the user interface for multi-user linking on Tenex.

tldr.problem: The current Tenex linking system works but offers a poor user experience when multiple users want to communicate together.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal changes how the RECEIVE LINKS and REFUSE LINKS states work. When two users link, both enter REFUSE LINKS state. A third user trying to link triggers a bell; if the first user accepts, all three users are linked together in a three-way conversation. Users leaving automatically revert to RECEIVE LINKS state.
tldr.outcome: The change gives a better user interface for multi-user conversations and would take only a couple of hours to implement. BBN had no objections to the current system, but said they would review the new approach if it proved successful.

today: RFC 576 is a proposal for a change to the Tenex operating system. It is not a standard or specification, but a request for feedback on a design modification.

sections.title: The Current Problem
sections.content: Tenex supports linking terminals for multi-user conversations, but the current interface is not ideal. Users can be in a RECEIVE LINKS state (ready to accept incoming links) or a REFUSE LINKS state (rejecting new links). The proposal aims to make conversations feel more natural by allowing existing participants to accept a new member into their conversation while rejecting random interruptions.
sections.plainLanguage: When two people are talking, the system should let them accept a third person into the conversation if they want, but not force them to.

sections.title: How the New System Works
sections.content: All users start in the default RECEIVE LINKS state. When user A and B link to each other, they enter a conversation and both move to REFUSE LINKS state, preventing random interruptions. When user C tries to link, a bell rings on A and B's terminals. If A ignores it, C is rejected and A and B continue. If A presses RECEIVE LINKS while the bell is ringing, C is linked into the entire conversation, and now all three are linked to each other in REFUSE LINKS state. When any user leaves by pressing BREAK LINKS, they return to RECEIVE LINKS state, and if they were the last member of a pair, the other person also returns to RECEIVE LINKS.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people talking can accept a third into the conversation with a bell alert and a single command. When someone leaves, they automatically go back to accepting links.

sections.title: System Implementation
sections.content: The change requires modifications to the TLINK system call to manage the new linking states. No changes are needed to the EXEC program. Additionally, the proposal adds a new system call that returns link and advise status for a terminal, showing which lines are linked to it, which it is linked to, and which lines are advising it. This information would be useful in status display programs and NLS for shared screen work. The proposal requests feedback within a couple of days and estimates only a couple of hours of implementation work.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a system-level change that will mostly involve updating one system call. A new command will also let programs check who is linked to whom.
